requirement:
# REQ-2297: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code.

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2297

#### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.
MessagePack generated code is not decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute.

Because it is very hard to write good coverage for generated MessagePack code, it may skew coverage numbers, especially on large projects with a lot of generated code.

#### Describe the solution you'd like
I would like all generated code to be decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute.  I do not feel like a setting is needed, but setting would be fine to have too.

#### Describe alternatives you've considered
There are no alternatives, it is close to impossible to write good coverage for generated code as it covers many edge cases.

#### Additional context

N/A

story.summary: The source generator's T4 templates (object formatter, string-key formatter, union, enum, resolver, composite resolver) and their compiled .cs files now put `[global::System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` on each generated formatter class. They also put it on the resolver class and on its nested helper classes (FormatterCache<T>, GetFormatterHelper). Every emission sits inside `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. TransformUtilities now writes a newline after the opening brace of a constrained nesting type, so the `#if` lands at the start of its own line. 222 snapshot files were regenerated. There are two new tests and a README note.
story.why: REQ-2297 asks for all generated code to carry ExcludeFromCodeCoverage so that generated formatters do not skew coverage numbers.
touches_beyond_requirement: TransformUtilities.EmitNestingTypesAndNamespaces now emits "{\r\n" instead of "{" for constrained nesting types. This changes whitespace in output that has nothing to do with the attribute, but it is needed so the preprocessor directive compiles.
README paragraph, which also states that the attribute is unavailable on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework.
story.confidence_overview: High that the templates and their .cs files emit the guarded attribute in the places shown. Medium that this meets the requirement: the `#if` guard drops the attribute for netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework consumers. ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute exists on those targets (.NET Framework 4.0+, netstandard2.0), so the guard looks unnecessary. The new tests are weak: one checks only that each generated file contains the attribute at least once. The enum and composite resolver templates are covered only by snapshot tests that do not appear in this diff.

The claim text also says guarded without explaining this TFM exclusion on the cited lines.

Claim C2 disputed: The requirement is only partly met: StringKeyFormatterTemplate.tt line 18 and StringKeyFormatterTemplate.cs line 37 wrap the attribute in #if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK, omitting ExcludeFromCodeCoverage on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework targets despite ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute being available in both netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework 4.0+. The claim also leaves the #if condition unexplained.

Claim C3 disputed: The requirement is only partly met: UnionTemplate.tt line 10 and UnionTemplate.cs line 30 guard the attribute with #if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK, omitting ExcludeFromCodeCoverage on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework targets even though ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute exists in both netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework 4.0+. The claim also does not explain the #if condition on the cited lines.

Claim C4 disputed: While the claim rightly notes that MyEnum in CodeCoverageExclusionTests.cs is unreferenced so EnumTemplate is not exercised there, the requirement is only partly met because EnumTemplate.tt line 8 and EnumTemplate.cs line 27 guard the attribute with #if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK, needlessly omitting ExcludeFromCodeCoverage on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework where the attribute is available.

Claim C5 disputed: Neither named test verifies that partial class <ResolverName> carries ExcludeFromCodeCoverage: the generated resolver file also emits the attribute on FormatterCache<T> and <ResolverName>GetFormatterHelper, and CodeCoverageExclusionTests.cs lines 75-77 and 91-95 only assert text.Contains(ExcludeAttribute), attributeCount > 0, and attributeCount == guardedCount, so both tests still pass if ResolverTemplate.tt lines 14-16 and ResolverTemplate.cs line 38 are removed. In addition, #if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK unnecessarily omits the attribute on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework.

Claim C6 disputed: The named test ExcludeAttributeIsGuardedForTargetsWhereItIsUnavailable (CodeCoverageExclusionTests.cs lines 91-95) does not test that FormatterCache<T> or <ResolverName>GetFormatterHelper receive ExcludeFromCodeCoverage: because partial class <ResolverName> already emits one guarded attribute in the same file, removing ResolverTemplate.tt lines 31-33 and 48-50 (ResolverTemplate.cs lines 55-57 and 67) leaves attributeCount == 1 and guardedCount == 1, so the test still passes. Also, #if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK unnecessarily omits the attribute on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework.

Claim C7 disputed: Although the claim accurately notes that neither new test exercises composite resolvers, the requirement is only partly met because CompositeResolverTemplate.tt lines 7 and 35 and CompositeResolverTemplate.cs lines 27 and 56 wrap ExcludeFromCodeCoverage in #if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK, omitting it on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework targets where ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute is available.

Claim C10 disputed: Cited line 18 of CodeCoverageExclusionTests.cs states the false premise that ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute is not available on netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework (it exists in both netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework 4.0+), and lines 82-97 enforce the #if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK guard that prevents the requirement from being met on those targets.

Claim C13 disputed: README.md line 1640 documents that ExcludeFromCodeCoverage is only emitted for targets where it is available (not netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework), which is factually incorrect because System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute is available in both netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework 4.0+ (only its unused Justification property requires .NET 5+).

The `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` guard (repeated in every template) suppresses the attribute for netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework consumers. System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute exists on .NET Framework 4.0+ and netstandard2.0, and applying it to classes is allowed there. Libraries targeting netstandard2.0, which are common for MessagePack users, would still have generated code counted in coverage, contrary to 'all generated code'.

The attribute is now emitted on the user's partial resolver class, and CompositeResolverTemplate.tt line 8 does the same. ExcludeFromCodeCoverage has AllowMultiple=false, so a user who already applied [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] to their own partial resolver declaration (an obvious workaround for this issue) will now hit duplicate-attribute error CS0579.

AllGeneratedTypesAreExcludedFromCodeCoverage only checks that each file contains the attribute somewhere. A missing attribute on FormatterCache<T> or GetFormatterHelper, or on one of several types in a file, would not fail it. The comment at line 69 claims an enum formatter is generated, but MyEnum is not referenced by any serialized member, so the enum template is likely untested here.

The new tests discard the output compilation and diagnostics, so they never verify that the generated code with `#if` directives compiles. The `{#if` problem fixed in TransformUtilities is caught only by snapshot tests outside this diff.
The README states the attribute is not available on netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework, which appears factually incorrect. Test comment line 18 repeats the claim.

Emitting [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] on the user-declared partial class <ResolverName> (and likewise in CompositeResolverTemplate.tt line 8) is a breaking compile error (CS0579: Duplicate 'ExcludeFromCodeCoverage' attribute) if the consumer already decorated their own resolver partial class declaration with [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage], because ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute specifies AllowMultiple = false and C# merges attributes across partial declarations. It also excludes any user-written methods on that partial class from coverage.

All 6 templates guard [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] with #if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK (and README.md line 1640 claims the attribute does not exist there), but parameterless System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute has existed since .NET Framework 4.0 (System.dll) and .NET Standard 2.0 (netstandard.dll); only its unused Justification property was added in .NET 5.0. Projects targeting netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework (such as net472/net48) needlessly get no coverage exclusion on generated code.

AllGeneratedTypesAreExcludedFromCodeCoverage asserts generated.Count >= 5 expecting formatters for MyObject, MyStringKeyObject, MyEnum, IMyUnion, plus the resolver (per line 69), but it passes only because [MessagePackObject] on MyUnionMember generates a 5th file (MyUnionMemberFormatter.g.cs), masking that no enum formatter was generated. Additionally, RunGeneratorAsync on line 123 discards the updated compilation and never asserts zero C# compiler diagnostics on the generated trees.
